planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, sharply drained gravelly soil in full sun, where strong light deepens the rosette toward its darkest plum-purple color.

directions: Press offsets directly onto the surface of very well-drained, gritty, mineral soil in full sun, since any lingering moisture around the crown invites rot. Rosettes hold a rich wine-purple to deep plum tone through most of the growing season, intensifying with cooler nights and fading toward green in heavy shade. It offsets steadily on short stolons, forming a dense mat that fills rock garden pockets and trough plantings within a couple of seasons. As with all hens and chicks, winter wet is more dangerous than winter cold, so avoid sites where water can pool around the crown.

planting.note: Plant offsets on the surface of sharply drained, lean gravelly soil in full sun; the pale, frosted rosette color is brightest in cold weather and strong light.

directions: Grow in gritty, mineral-rich soil with sharp drainage and full sun, since standing moisture around the crown is far more damaging than cold. The tightly packed rosette carries a silvery, frost-dusted blue-green cast that turns whiter and more pronounced as temperatures drop in fall and winter. It offsets freely on short stolons, gradually forming a dense clump suited to troughs, crevice gardens, and rock wall pockets. Individual rosettes are monocarpic and die after flowering, but the surrounding offsets continue the planting indefinitely.

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of sharply drained gravelly soil in full sun, where soft peach-pink tones develop best against the muted green rosette base.

directions: Grow in lean, sharply drained gritty soil in full sun, which brings out the gentle peach-pink blush along the leaf tips against soft green undertones. The rosette stays compact and rounded, offsetting readily on short stolons to knit into a low mat over a season or two. Like other hens and chicks, it tolerates drought and poor soil far better than wet feet, so avoid sites where winter rain can pool around the crown. Afternoon shade in the hottest summer climates can help preserve the softer color tones from bleaching out.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; cool weather and strong light bring out the softest violet-grey tones in the rosette.

directions: Grow in fast-draining, gritty soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot inland climates, since intense heat can bleach the muted lavender-grey overlay from the rosette. Branching stems carry rounded rosettes in soft dove-grey shading into a faint violet blush toward the leaf margins, a subtler coloring than the near-black or bright red aeonium cultivars more commonly grown. Like other aeoniums it grows actively through the cool, wet months and rests through summer heat, so water regularly from fall through spring and taper off sharply once temperatures climb. Propagate easily from stem cuttings allowed to callus for a few days before rooting in dry, gritty mix.
